utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment before you bring the witness in I'm sorry we're starting late today. Apparently the previous case overran. I've had no official word of why that was or the circumstances, but I've had unofficially that that's the explanation for our delayed start. I want to raise two other matters before we start again with evidence. The first of these relates to the translation of documents, and an e-mail was sent suggesting that there should be a meeting on Thursday at 1.00 to try to resolve this once and for all so that there's a clear agreement on how we progress to ensure that everyone gets documents at the best possible time. For us to have an administrative meeting of this nature, it doesn't appear to us necessary that the accused should be present, but we would only have such a meeting that might affect a number of the accused in their absence with the agreement of the accused. Can we take it that all counsel and their clients are happy to have that meeting in the absence of the accused? That enables us to have it without using valuable in-court time, so that will be at 1.00 on Thursday. I don't know whether the place has been confirmed, but it will be one of the meeting rooms. Although it affects specifically three accused, all counsel may attend, at least one counsel from each team and the Prosecution may attend if they wish, and representatives of CLSS and OLAD have also been invited to attend. The other matter I wish to raise relates to the evidence. Mr. Ackerman, you've raised a question over the reference to exhibits in your 92 ter statements. Now, I looked at this yesterday and probably should have raised it although I didn't. Can you give me an example of this from yesterday's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think there is one in yesterday's evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's reassuring because what had happened yesterday was that there was an indication that you may refer to exhibits, but I had no recollection of any actually appearing in the statement. I think what we should do is when this arises specifically, draw the Bench's attention to it and we'll be able to give clear guidance so that there's no misunderstanding. But I would anticipate that if an exhibit number appears in the statement and there's an indication of something in the statement about it, that it would normally be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. In order to try to make effective use of 92 ter statements to save time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- We thought it would save time if we didn't have to show exhibits to the witness and have them say, yeah, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Thank you. Our next witness is Stanimir Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to greet everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, is there a statement under Rule 92 ter for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is. I believe it's in the e-court system and the number is 4D502.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll get one printed off for myself and anyone else who hasn't got it. I certainly have not seen this one, and I've just noticed that he's a -- there will be reference in his evidence to a statement. Mr. Radosavljevic, you will now be examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir, can you tell us your full name, for the record. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Stanimir Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of September, did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read that statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I read it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And if the same questions were asked of you today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement is 4D502 and I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colleague Radosavljevic, would you tell the Trial Chamber briefly about your career and the various posts you occupied.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Your Honour, Presiding Judge, Your Honours, you see in my statement that I was born in 1948, I finished high school and law school at the university, passed my bar exam, served in the army, graduated from the infantry school of reserve officers while in the army, after which I was promoted into active duty officer in the rank of lieutenant, and I became an active-duty serviceman. During my active service, I completed military political school. After an apprenticeship at the military prosecutor's office in Nis and the military court, I was assigned to my first job at the command of the operations group in Pristina, that was the precursor of the Pristina Corps, I was legal affairs officer there, and my job was actually to represent military units and military institutions in courts all over Kosovo and Metohija. I continued in that job from 1975 to 1982, when I was appointed deputy military prosecutor in Nis. I stayed in that post until 1992, when I was appointed military prosecutor in Nis. I remained in that position until May 2005, when the military justice system was definitively liquidated. In the meantime during the war in 1999, I had been assigned deputy military prosecutor at the supreme military prosecutor's office at the 3rd Army in Nis. Since 2005 I have been a lawyer with my own practice in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to clarify one thing for me, please. In paragraph 5 of your statement you tell us that in wartime the first-instance courts are established in each of the army's corps' districts and so on, and then in paragraph 11 you tell us of five of these being established. Are these the five that you had responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those were first-instance military prosecutor's offices in the territory of the command of the 3rd Army, whereas the district of the military prosecutor's office in Nis -- sorry, the section of the military prosecutor's office in Nis was a second-instance organ relative to those prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your duties as deputy supreme military prosecutor, did they extend throughout Serbia or were you confined to the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They applied to the territory of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colleague Radosavljevic, for the duration of the war as deputy military prosecutor in the deputy of the military prosecutor attached to the command of the 3rd Army, to whom were you answerable for your work?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was answerable to the supreme military prosecutor attached to the Supreme Command Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was in that position?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was General Svetomir Obrencevic, major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You have already answered the Presiding Judge, saying that you had within your jurisdiction first-instance military prosecutors of those five offices in Kosovo. Was it their duty to report to you on their work?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the stipulation, and I had requested that they inform me daily on the number of new cases, number of investigations, and new charges brought for each day, and they did that regularly. Therefore, I received that information, organized it, and submitted it to the assistant commander for legal affairs of the 3rd Army as a daily brief on developments in crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you have to report to the supreme military prosecutor in any way?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The supreme military prosecutor did not ask me to report on a daily basis, but I had the obligation to send such a report to the legal department of the headquarters of the supreme staff, which I did, to the Supreme Command Staff I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was in that position during the war?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: At that time it was Major-General Gojovic. I can't recall his first name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Relative to reporting by first-instance military prosecutor's offices that were subordinate to you, did their reports contain information that anybody tried to pressurise them in their work as to how they should proceed in specific cases or not? Would you please wait for my question to finish.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: May I? There were no such reports, ever. I toured Prosecutor's offices, both in Nis and in Pristina. I toured the one in Nis several times and the one in Pristina twice, so I was in the field personally. I had personal contact with prosecutors and their deputies, and nobody ever mentioned any problem of that kind to me. They informed me of the cases they were handling and of their work in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: How about you personally, did you feel any pressure along the chain of command or maybe through the line of security organs? Were you under any pressure as deputy military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it never happened; and if it had, I would certainly have informed the supreme military prosecutor. That never happened, either in peacetime or during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colleague, would you please tell the Court, under the Law on the Military Prosecutor's Offices and the Law on Criminal Proceedings, on whom lies the primary responsibility for detection of perpetrators of criminal offences and their preparations for prosecution and trial?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Military prosecutors certainly followed the Law on Criminal Proceedings in their work and also the Law on Military Courts. The Law on Criminal Proceedings, which is the only law governing criminal proceedings in our country, stipulates the obligation to file criminal reports in this way. Every citizen should file a criminal report when necessary, but that is not an obligation for the citizen. It is a -- more of a recommendation, it is desirable. On the other hand, it is stipulated that state authorities are duty-bound to file a criminal report when they found out about a crime in their line of work. Thirdly, it is prescribed precisely which state authorities are engaged in detecting crimes and filing criminal reports and charges. Under the law, it's the organs of the interior or, to put it simply, the police. The Law on Military Courts, on the other hand, prescribes that the powers and obligations of the organs of internal affairs before military courts have military security organs and military police. They are the equivalent of the civilian police before civilian courts, and in practice on the basis of my experience in the military justice system, which is over 20 years, they did so regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your work as deputy military prosecutor, did you ever come to meet a person called Lakic Djorovic?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did meet him, but not before an incident in which he committed a criminal offence, for which he was later prosecuted. I can give you details or maybe you want to ask me questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Before that, would you tell the Trial Chamber, what was the position of Mr. Lakic Djorovic at the moment when you met him?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Lakic Djorovic was at the time military prosecutor attached to the military district of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: How long before the incident was he appointed to that duty, if you know?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I know that it was not more than a week before the incident in question in which he committed the criminal offence which later resulted in his resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call on e-court 4D166.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you, Colleague, would you be so kind to look at it when it comes up on the screen and tell us if you are familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if that's the correct number. The statement previously indicated in Exhibit 4D166 and when we looked for it we couldn't find it in e-court. I was told it was 4D159.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. My mistake. I see that it's 4D159. My mistake, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radosavljevic, do you know this document?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell something more about the document?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received this report some time after the 1st of June, maybe even on the 1st of June but I don't think so. It was rather after the 1st of June. It was a report from the military prosecutor, from the command of the military district, it's a report by Lakic Djorovic about the work of his agency for that period. He informed me about the number of open cases, number of investigations, number of indictments, and I received it as such. Of course as far as I recall that report contained no reference whatsoever to any problems that this prosecutor's office was experiencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please now go back to that incident when you had first met Mr. Lakic Djorovic and tell the Trial Chamber what exactly happened and what he told you.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to give you more details about that. I don't know the exact date, but it was sometime in the first half of May when I -- when the chief of the legal administration of the Supreme Command Staff, Mr. Gojovic, came to inspect and tour the military justice organs in Nis. He toured the courts, and then he decided it's also advisable to visit the military prosecutor's offices in Pristina, and so we did. It was decided then that at the military prosecutor's office attached to the command in Pristina we have a deputy who is much more experienced than the prosecutor himself, so it would be a good idea to appoint someone else to be the prosecutor. Until that time it was Lieutenant Djuro Blagojevic, who was relatively low in rank and had relatively little experience, while his deputies were much more experienced, and that was one of the major reasons to appoint somebody with more experience. General Gojovic said that he would make efforts to find appropriate persons in Belgrade who would be eligible for that appointment. I later found out that they found a candidate, namely Lakic Djorovic, and he was indeed appointed. However, what happened was that - when did this happen? On the 30th - towards the end of May, I'm not sure exactly, an incident happened. Lakic Djorovic got drunk on official premises in the presence of his deputies. Then he beat up his deputy, causing grievous bodily injury. After that, the police intervened; however, he barricaded himself on the premises of the prosecutor's office and threatened the police with a pistol. The military police withdrew. Later on in a way that I'm not familiar with, he nevertheless stopped doing what it was he was doing until then. In relation to this, General Obrencevic, the supreme military prosecutor ordered me to go from Nis to Pristina and to interview all the participants in this incident, which I did. I went to Pristina and I spoke to all of them, inter alia, to Lakic Djorovic, that is to say, the prosecutor. He was making excuses for himself, saying that the deputy had offended him with certain words, and that was it as far as his defence was concerned, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: May I? In addition to that he just told me -- are you allowing me to go on? He said that he had problems because he did not have an appropriate vehicle and he was struggling to get an appropriate vehicle for his use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, is it your testimony that while he was on duty as the military, or rather, that it was less than a week that he was military prosecutor in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said around a week. Now, was it a week exactly or six days, I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Fine. That will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please call up on e-court 4D171.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colleague, would you please look at this material. Can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see, this is information of the military prosecutor in Nis from 2001; that is to say, information that was compiled after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that compiled this information?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know, I compiled it, of course with the assistance of my officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly how it was that this information was compiled and what is the information contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed I cannot remember exactly why it was that this information was compiled, because this is not regular information. Every month the prosecutor would compile regular monthly documents called information about crime tendencies; however, since this refers to the period of the war, I assume that it was the army command or somebody else, say the supreme military prosecutor, who say that I do this for the army command, so I did that. That is to say that I compiled this information about crime tendencies in this field, in this area, for that period of time, the time of the war, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this still on the subject of Djorovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you go into this any further can I clarify with you, Mr. Aleksic, first of all, paragraph 16 of the statement which refers at the end to the request for removal P2753 and 4D159. Now, 4D159 is the number you've now given to the report for the period from 1st March -- 23rd March to 1st June. Is the reference in paragraph 16 accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that there has been a mistake in terms of numbers. 4D166 from paragraph 15 is this request of Lakic Djorovic's to be relieved of duty. I am going to deal with this, and we shall notify you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And the other matter I want to ask is a question for the witness. Mr. Radosavljevic, what happened with your report after you had investigated Djorovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not investigate, if I understood correctly what it was that you said, when I paid this visit; I just conducted an interview with him. I did not compile a note on that because by then the military police had taken over the matter to deal with the pre-trial procedure. After that, an investigation was instituted against him and charges were brought against him for two crimes, perhaps even a third one, one being grievous bodily injury and the other one was assault against a military officer while on duty, because it is with weapons that he attacked the military police. Proceedings against him were carried out before the military court in Nis, and as far as I know the trial is not over yet. It is now a civilian court in Belgrade that is in charge of the matter, or rather, I'm not quite sure in which city this is happening, whether it's Belgrade or Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your understanding is that there's no result as yet. We've had a fair bit of evidence from Djorovic himself about this. You'll appreciate why I'm asking. The other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. And for the avoidance of doubt, I assumed you had carried out an investigation when you said that you were ordered to go to Pristina and interview all the participants, which you did, but that was an internal matter. That wasn't an investigation of the incident itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was not an investigation on the incident itself. It was getting personal information about what it was that had happened. I spoke to the participants personally to find out what it was that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic, back to 4D171 then?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, the document that is referred to in paragraph 16, the exact number would be P2753. The rest should be deleted. And as for paragraph 15, it is number 159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's already been clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colleague, I'm Djuro Cepic, Defence counsel for General Lazarevic. Just one question. During the war, how many criminal reports did you receive per day on average?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand this question to be a question meaning how many criminal reports the first-instance prosecutors received, because I as deputy supreme prosecutor did not receive any criminal reports. According to the information that I received then and in terms of the sum of all the criminal reports pertaining to that period of time, there were some days when 100 or even 150 reports would be received per day, sometimes 30 only, but on average about 100 reports per day at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the overall number at the level of the 3rd Army, do you know perhaps how many reports were received? I'm just speaking in approximate terms.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that the prosecutor of the Pristina Corps only received over 2 and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, that will do. Thank you. Thank you very much. That was my last question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I haven't got any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. You'll now be examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You retired as --

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You retired as a colonel I understand?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I retired as a colonel because military prosecutor's offices and courts ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And may I call you "Colonel" because it's easier for me to pronounce than your last name?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in an earlier answer that the military -- I think your answer was translated as the military justice system was liquidated in 2005. Does that mean that there are no more military courts or military prosecutors in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Military courts ceased to exist on the 31st of December, 2004, that is to say that already by the 1st of January, 2005, they were no longer in existence; however, the personnel, part of the personnel, stayed on in these organs until May 2005 in order to have the liquidation process of these organs take place, from an administrative point of view, et cetera. However, the organs as such, the judiciary as such, ceased to exist from the end of 2004, since then there have been no such courts. However, today there are military departments attached to courts in Nis and Belgrade, that is the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it then that those military departments attached to the courts handled the work of prosecuting violations within the military by members of the military, correct?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. They are within the district organ that is called the district public prosecutor's office. There is not a head of this military department. There are only a few deputy prosecutors who carry out those duties in that department. They are subordinated to the district public prosecutor. They do not have any other superior except for that person, and they act in accordance with his orders. Of course, in practice they deal with all cases that the district public prosecutor's office inherited, so to speak, from the military court, but they also deal with other cases from the regular jurisdiction of the district court, or rather, the district prosecutor's office. I personally know that before this department to this day some proceedings are taking place that had started originally before the military court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer to Judge Bonomy, a question about your duties as the deputy supreme military prosecutor, you said they applied to the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army. Do I take it then that in addition to yourself there were in 1999 some other deputy supreme military prosecutors that had responsibility in other areas, such as for the 1st and 2nd Armies?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In Nis in addition to myself there was another deputy, and I think that in Podgorica there was also one. I'm not quite sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the other deputy in Nis with you?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade too, yes, in Podgorica and Belgrade. The other deputy in Nis was Radonja Zivkovic, he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how was the work split between the two of you in Nis?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Since I had senior rank, I decided who would take what case, which cases I would be working on and which cases he would be working on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then you mentioned that the supreme military prosecutor attached to the Supreme Command Staff in Belgrade was Major-General Obrencevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then I take it is he then the top dog or the one and only overall supreme prosecutor for the whole VJ at that time?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Before that, in peacetime, he was the chief military prosecutor, that is to say the top prosecutor in the land, and he was that during the course of the war, too. Once he came to tour the prosecutor's offices in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that although he didn't ask you to report, you did send reports to the legal department of the headquarters of the supreme staff. Now, was that a separate report or was that report something that was integrated in the daily combat reports from the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: These were telephone reports every day. I informed them by telephone that on such and such a day we received such and such a number of reports, brought such and such a number of charges against persons, dealt with such and such a number of cases. That is what General Obrencevic asked me to do, to send the legal department this kind of information in order to have all the information centralised about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were those the only kind of reports you submitted then were the telephonic reports, no written reports?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, during the course of the war I did not write reports. As a matter of fact, that is when we stopped writing monthly information after decades of having done so. For decades we wrote monthly information documents, but then due to the war that was going on we did not write this up. Nobody asked us to do this. I think I even asked, but they told me that it was not necessary to write this monthly information at that point in time. It was an enormous number, several thousand per month, so it was very difficult to process everything, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned to Mr. Aleksic that in your tours of the prosecutor's office under you, that you had personal contact with the prosecutors and their deputies and nobody ever mentioned any problem of the kind of being pressured in their work. I understand that no one told you that, but my question is: Were you specifically inquiring or asking any of them if they had that kind of problem?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I was not inquiring or asking. It never crossed my mind. I do not believe, and to this day I do not believe, that there was such pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it, though, that you're familiar with some of the allegations that Colonel Djorovic made when he testified here about pressures that were put on him, correct?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I just heard in very general terms that he referred to some pressures, but I really do not know specifically what it was that he was saying and what kind of pressure he was referring to before the court, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of his allegation about pressure being put on him to initiate some kind of proceeding against Natasa Kandic from the International Humanitarian Law centre or the Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is a completely different area. That is what he said about 2001 and not about 1999 and that can be checked when you look at the evidence he gave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time he was not the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, can you be more specific about the time to which you're referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the date in front of me. I will get that and come back to it if I have it; if not, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it then your earlier answers about no pressure is referring specifically to 1999, but I also take it from an earlier answer that cases from the conflict in Kosovo in 1999, some matters are still being pursued through the courts, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the information I have. I personally had contact with a person a few days ago because he was a witness in this case a few days ago, and he told me that this day there are proceedings against him in terms of a trial that had started against him before the military court in Nis. Allegedly he had been sentenced, but then the judgement was annulled and there was a retrial and proceedings are now taking place before the district court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was that person you had this contact with?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Zlatan Mancic, I think he is a lieutenant-colonel from the KVO -- no, sorry, from the military department in Pirot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of proceedings were being had against him for what alleged charges?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Believe me that I do not recall the details, but I think that it's a war crime, I think, I'm not sure. And if this case was dealt with with the -- by the military court in Nis and the military prosecutor's office in Nis, I think that as prosecutor on this case several times I asked for additional information and that we lost quite a bit of time on that before we decided to bring criminal charges against him and to start a court procedure against him. It is probable that this procedure started a bit later because of that, but that is certainly not the reason why the proceedings haven't been completed as yet. The reason must be that the truth has not been established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you yourself in your work as a military prosecutor from 1999 on, did you never experience any pressure in connection with your work, pressure to take a specific course of action with regard to a matter pending before you from a superior or a higher-ranking officer in the army?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I categorically assert that this, indeed, never happened to me. Absolutely no pressure whatsoever. Interest was expressed in terms of how far a particular case had progressed, but pressure in terms of how a decision would be made, that kind of thing never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to handle a matter against a journalist named Filipovic, Miroslav Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I personally handled that matter initially, and later on it was my deputy who continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that matter involved some allegations that he was, what, revealing state secrets or speaking negatively about the army? What were the natures -- the nature of the charges against him?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're asking me what it was that he was accused of. I think for revealing a military secret. I'm not sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I have a general objection in respect of this question and similar questions. According to the laws of the country that I come from and the witness comes from, court cases are not to be commented upon. A court is independent in its activity, and any kind of interpretation by anyone who is not relevant from that point of view can only be to the detriment of those proceedings. As far as I believe, there is a similar rule before this Tribunal, namely, contempt of court. This is my general objection, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, one of the issues before this Tribunal is whether or not proceedings were taken in circumstances where they should have been taken, which of course inevitably involves investigating the nature of charges. Now, this is very similar, although it may not be to do with the crimes of the nature that we would have jurisdiction over. So on the basis -- on the understanding that the questions are confined to what the charges were and what the outcome was, what really is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to repeat. It is not permitted to comment upon the course of the proceedings because the court is independent in its activity. That is in accordance with our law, the laws of the country that I come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I could never ask in a court in Belgrade whether a witness had previously been convicted of a crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that's a completely different matter, Your Honour. Evidence is a completely, or rather, records are a completely different matter and a judgement is a completely different matter. But the course of the proceedings and affecting the course of the proceedings and interpreting the course of the proceedings is solely within the jurisdiction of those who are in charge, that is to say the court and the judge involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no -- I don't have that kind of objection, but I believe that those proceedings against journalist Filipovic was proclaimed to be a state secret at some point and some of the evidence was confidential, it was not in the public domain, and I believe perhaps we should move into private session for that reason. I do not object to the questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying the very fact that he was prosecuted was a state secret?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there may come a time when it's necessary, but it's not necessary at this stage. Mr. Hannis, can you respond to the first of these objections from Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm not trying to get into the contents of these charges. I have an interest because I have a good-faith basis to ask a question about whether this witness received any kind of pressure based on his conduct in the case. I have a media report indicating that he had ordered the release of this individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to say any more at this stage. We're alert to the point that Mr. Cepic is making and if the issue appears to specifically arise in relation to any question, then he will no doubt draw it to our attention, but we may be alerted to it in any event by the nature of the objection he's already taken. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it correct, Colonel, that in connection with Mr. Filipovic at one point in time you did order that he be released from detention?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not order his release from detention; that was not within my competence. I just informed the court that I would not be filing a request for an investigation within 48 hours, because at that moment I thought a prosecution would not be justified. That is why the court was bound by the law to release him from detention and that's what they did as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. It was because you took the decision not to request an investigation within the 48-hour time-limit, he had to be released, correct?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That was stipulated by the law. If no request to conduct an investigation is filed within 48 hours, then the person has to be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you hear of any complaints of General Pavkovic about your actions that led to the release of Mr. Filipovic that were reported in the media?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear about any complaints as far as that is concerned, but I can tell you that my decision not to request an investigation testifies to my complete independence and the fact that I did not consult anyone, I didn't ask the staff [as interpreted], I decided it on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that other prosecutors may not have the same degree of resilience or persistence as you?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I really could not go into that. People are people. Everyone answers for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, just one correction to the record. Page 25, or rather, line 25, the witness said something that was misheard by the interpreter as "staff," where he actually said: I didn't ask anyone what to do. There is a difference of one sound, one letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radosavljevic, can you clarify that answer? You said that your decision not to question an investigation testifies to your independence and the fact that you did not consult, who did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about that situation with that report, those charges that had to be filed or not filed. I didn't ask anyone what to do. I studied the case myself, then decided to inform the court as I did, that I will not be conducting an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A little earlier in your evidence you said that you personally had contact with a person a few days ago because he was a witness in this case a few days ago and he told me that this day there are proceedings against him in terms of a trial in Nis, and you then referred to the person as Zlatan Mancic. I don't think that's the name of a witness we've had in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, you misunderstood me. He wasn't a witness in this case. He's a witness in one of my cases that I am handling as a private lawyer in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, in answer to a question at page 8, line 9, you mentioned how military prosecutors followed the law on criminal proceedings, and you mentioned that in your country every citizen should file a criminal report when necessary but it's not an obligation for the citizen. "On the other hand," you say, "it is stipulated that state authorities are duty-bound to file a criminal report when they found out about a crime in their line of work." When General Gojovic was here we had a discussion about that with him, and I want to propose a hypothetical situation for you and ask you what responsibility, if any, there is for a military commander in Kosovo during the conflict, he has an area of responsibility, he has information that MUP units or individuals from the MUP who are working in coordination with VJ troops in that area, may have committed crimes against civilians, including murder, rape, robbery. What responsibility does that VJ commander have with regard to doing something about crimes committed by MUP members not subordinated to him but in his area of responsibility? Does he only have the citizen's moral obligation?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood the question easily. Now it's a matter of interpreting the law. My understanding would be that it does not -- he is not obligated, but he should report it. You could say that 15 different agencies should file a report simultaneously if 15 of them find about an incident. When I say that the state authority's obligated, I mean that the state authority is obligated to file a report on an irregularity or a crime they found out in their line of work. For instance, the electrical company is not the one who should be filing a report if something happened at the health centre. In the same way, the commander of a military unit is not obligated to file a report if he finds out that a policeman who is not serving in the army committed a crime. I think it's a matter for interpretation. But I do not mean to say that he should not. I'm saying that it's not his formal obligation, but he should report it in whatever form, maybe not through a formal criminal report, but he should go and tell the body, the agency, of the -- of internal affairs in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I just have to clarify one thing. If once a report about an incident is made, is there a need for many other people also to go and report the same incident? Or if -- once it is done, it is okay, or in your system 40 complaints on the same episode can be made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. For the work of a military prosecutor [as interpreted], a criminal report is not necessary. It is enough that the military prosecutor finds out that a criminal offence has been perpetrated. If the word reaches me at all, if I find out in the street that somebody killed somebody, that is quite enough for me to take certain measures, to contact the police, find out if they know about the incident, have them take the steps, and start the prosecution. One criminal report is quite enough for me to find out and to start my work. If another 12 people file a criminal report about the same incident, that does not bother me, because every criminal report might mention some new detail, some new fact, a new piece of evidence. So to conclude, the military prosecutor does not require a formal criminal report; he just needs information, information that might reach him by telephone, verbally, in writing, in any possible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You also stated that the decisions were you own and nobody influenced you or pressurised you to go into investigation. But obviously, you are not a judge. You can be told that you are not investigating an event which has happened because of inaptitude on your part. What happens then? And there can be a pressure on you of work because there's a back-log and somebody's reminding you. So how do you distinguish between these positions because obviously you are not a judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, the question is how am I able to finalise a case. The answer is this: The military prosecutor is an independent body that prosecutes perpetrators of criminal offences, and that's the source of his right to reject a criminal report if he finds it unjustified. And that happens regularly in practice. In the practice of every prosecutor's office in the country, it has been established once and for all that a criminal report may be rejected by a formal decision, a decision saying the criminal report filed against such and such a person for such and such a reason is hereby rejected, and this is followed by an explanation. Of course this is not done automatically. The preliminary inquiries are first made from individuals, from institutions, from authorities, and on the basis of all the evidence obtained and all the statements available, the decision is made. And the court cannot help it. That is our system. If the prosecutor decides not a prosecute, it cannot reach the court, unless the injured party continues their effort to have the perpetrator prosecuted. We are also duty-bound to inform the injured party that they may institute proceedings on their own behalf within a certain deadline. It happens often that the injured party starts proceedings themselves, and in the course of those proceedings the military prosecutors rethink their prior decision to reject the case and take over. But a prosecution cannot happen without either the prosecutor or the injured party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And did somebody oversee your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I said, every month the prosecutor wrote a brief that was submitted to the supreme prosecutor about the developments and incidents of crime. In addition to that, the prosecutor made a sheet of statistics, including various elements, the rank, ethnicity of the perpetrator, the type of criminal offence, indictment, conviction, sentencing, et cetera. And at the end of the year, all those sheets were used to make an annual report. And the prosecutor provided every year an annual report on his work for the previous year --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Who's supervising you, could he correct you when you were not right in taking a decision one way or the other whether to proceed with the case or not to proceed with the case because you could have been wrong. Could he correct you and override your decision? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. Certainly. That would be the supreme military prosecutor. The organization of prosecutors are very strictly -- is very strictly established in terms of hierarchy. The supreme military prosecutor controls the work of military prosecutors, and it is his duty to provide guide-lines if they deem necessary, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had seen a couple of my colleagues across the hall up. I don't know if there were corrections to be made to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, just one small correction in the transcript page 28, line 21, I think the witness said just prosecutor, not the military prosecutor, as is filed the transcript. Thank you, because he spoke in general. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even if he did, it really is of no consequence in view of the answer. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This is the intervention page 30, 10, "it happened often." I don't believe -- the witness didn't say "often," he was just saying it might happen, even the case where the injured party takes on and then the prosecutor decides. It doesn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note the witness agrees with you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I wanted to follow-up a little bit. I understood your answer a while back, and I can see in the context of peacetime that an army commander who becomes aware that some policeman has committed a crime against the civilian might not have any obligation to do anything about that other than an ordinary citizen's duty or, if not duty, the idea that it would be a good thing to report that crime. But I'm talking about during the war in Kosovo in combat, and I understood from answers of earlier witnesses we've had that a military commander in a combat zone has responsibility to protect the civilians in his area of responsibility. Is that true? It seems logical to me.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter of interpreting the Geneva Conventions. I would not be prepared to go into that now. I can only say if the case happens during the war, during a war, and if the commanding officer finds out about a war crime, then he certainly should report it and I believe he would report it. But whether somebody's required to protect civilians and who, that must be governed by Geneva Conventions, and I wouldn't go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree with me in the situation of Kosovo in 1999, who was in a better position to protect the civilians than the army? The civilians didn't have -- I'm talking about the standard ordinary civilians didn't have weapons to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That's really outside of my expertise. I was not familiar with the details of the situation in the whole territory, but I believe there were -- there existed state authorities in Kosovo. I don't think the army was the authority in Kosovo. There was a government, a police force, and other organs who had that job. If there are some regulations stipulating that the army should protect the population, possibly, I'm not aware of it now. Of course their moral obligation would be to protect civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understood an earlier answer of yours to indicate that you as a prosecutor, if you became aware of a crime without the filing of any report, you just personally became aware of it, you would go ahead and initiate proceedings, correct? What would you do in the situation if you as a VJ military prosecutor became aware that a MUP officer or a MUP soldier had committed a crime against a civilian in Kosovo during the war, what would you do about that?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood your question. My conduct would depend on several things. For instance, it would depend on my evaluation, whether the report is reliable, whether it is a report or disinformation. If I thought it reliable, I would make an official note as a prosecutor, and then I would submit that official note to the competent prosecutor. If the urgent -- if there is urgency in the matter, I would certainly contact the competent prosecutor by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I understood from other evidence that in this context the military courts did not have jurisdiction over the MUP policemen or the PJP or the SAJ policemen who was engaged in activities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course they did not have jurisdiction. The Law on Military Courts stipulates their jurisdiction very precisely, that is, to prosecute military personnel and in very specific cases other persons. For instance, in cases where the injured party is a military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Even if the perpetrator is a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From your earlier answer then where you said that you would make an official note as the prosecutor and submit that official note to the competent prosecutor, in my hypothetical -- let me take it a step further. Your information about the crime is either one that you've seen yourself or it's in a written report by, say, General Lazarevic, to his commander in the 3rd Army. Would that satisfy you as sufficient evidence that a crime had occurred and to whom would you report it? Would you report it to a civilian court prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you correctly, if I found out from a certain document of General Lazarevic that he had done such and such a thing, I would consider it reliable or if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood, Mr. Radosavljevic. You're being asked still about the situation where a MUP officer commits a crime and you've got reliable information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your information is a written report from General Lazarevic, who, I'm assuming, would be a reliable source for you about that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I understood, that the crime was committed by a policeman and that General Lazarevic is writing about it to his command in Nis. And if I found out about it, the question is addressed to me, what would I do and would I act identically. The answer is yes. I did not distinguish in my previous answer between various sources I might find out from. Regardless of the source of this report, I would inform the prosecutor, the competent prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who would that be, the competent prosecutor, for a crime committed during the wartime by a MUP member against a civilian in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The competent prosecutor would be determined according to the territory. It's territorial competence that governs these matters, the territory where the crime was committed. Those were the same prosecutors to whom we actually deferred cases for which we were not competent, the civilian prosecutors in the area, the locality of perpetration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were those courts working during the war in March through June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: These courts, yes. I said yes. I didn't deal with it specifically, but I believe they did work and I believe they continued to work after the end of the war after being relocated to Serbia proper. So we sent them the cases in which we deemed ourselves incompetent or not qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9 of your statement you say: "Military courts only had jurisdiction to try military offences perpetrated by military personnel, cases in relation to service in the VJ, and some civilians in specific situations." What were the specific situations under which you in the military courts had jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Law on Military Courts lists such crimes. It is said the military courts shall try the following criminal offences: Espionage, sabotage, subversion of offence, capacities, et cetera. Espionage, but only if against military installation or military personnel, divulging military secrets. Other acts that go against the army has a social value. I would actually have to take an exam again to see if I know all of these, but I believe I recollected correctly. There are about a dozen different offences that are considered to go against the country and its defence capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a list of criminal reports against perpetrators in the 549th Motorised Brigade, it's Exhibit P962, and I see one of the crimes listed is a violation of Articles 125 and 136 of the criminal code for FRY and it's described as terrorism and association for hostile purposes. Was that something that you could try?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was within our jurisdiction, again, if such an act violated the defence capabilities and security of the country. There were numerous cases wherein Albanians attacked the army, the state border, the -- involving smuggling of weapons, et cetera, so I considered them as terrorism and prosecuted them as such. Of course, unfortunately, we were not successful in many cases because we decided that we did not have enough evidence and we instructed the police to continue their work to detect -- to detect the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think it's time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radosavljevic, we need to have a break at this stage for a number of reasons. I wonder if you would leave the court with the usher, and we'll see you again at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, in your statement at paragraph 20 you mentioned that: "... According to the law, the Court is not bound by the legal qualification made by the Prosecutor in the indictment, but only by the facts; therefore, the Court can amend the legal qualification and decide that some alternative offence is more appropriate. This may result in a lack of jurisdiction and the case will be delegated to the appropriate court." Is there any appeal or remedy a prosecutor could take if the court decided to change the legal qualification of the charges that might result in it going away, say, away from the military court to a civilian court or is that something the court can do and it's not appealable?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, an appeal can be filed, certainly. If the prosecutor is not satisfied with the ruling of the court from any point of view, he has the right to appeal in that sense as well, in terms of the change of the legal qualification, that part of the judgement, in this way, the ruling on jurisdiction as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned also in the next paragraph that once the war stops the war military courts are discontinued. And if an indictment hasn't yet been delivered to a suspect and that suspect is no longer a military person, for example, because he's been demobilised, then the regular civilian court has jurisdiction. What about -- what if the indictment has been delivered and the suspect's then demobilised, does the case still go to the civilian court because he's no longer a soldier?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: "Argumentu a contrario" in that case the court is in charge if it is a valid indictment and he is still a military person, the matter remains within the military court and the military court is going to bring the proceedings to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But I was imagining a situation where the indictment has been delivered to him while he's still in the army, but then the war ends. Is he automatically demobilised or does that take some sort of order or decree to be issued for the mobilisation to take effect?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm to give a right answer to when he is no longer a military person. When the military unit ceases to exist, he ceases to be a military person. A person becomes a military person by acceding to a military unit and also ceases to be a military person by getting out of the unit, or rather, through the fact that this unit ceases to exist. I don't know exactly when each unit ceased to exist. However, I believe that once the state of war was over, these mobilised units ceased to exist as well. Therefore, when the state of war is over, when there are no more mobilised units, I think this happens automatically without any formal decisions, rulings, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then would I be correct in assuming that any soldier who had been mobilised simply for the war, once the war ended and his unit is automatically demobilised, the military court no longer has jurisdiction over any of those demobilised individuals, whether or not the indictment had already been passed on and delivered to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The law clearly states that the court shall remain in charge if the indictment remains valid or if the proposal to indict had been officially delivered to the court. We cannot interpret it in any other way but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if the indictment was delivered before demobilisation, the military court can continue to prosecute that person until the end of the case and pass a sentence on him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, certainly, until a judgement is delivered, not only that military court but even the second-instance court, an appeals court, until the judgement becomes valid [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, may I intervene. I hope you don't mind. Now, if there's a mixture of accused, let's say two from MUP, two from VJ, and they commit a crime, which court is going to have jurisdiction then if they -- through, you know, concert and premeditation or they join in a crime? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That question is also resolved in the Law on Military Courts. It stipulates that if a military and a non-military person, say, a military policeman and a policeman commit a crime as co-perpetrators, the military person shall be tried by the military court but the other person will also be tried by that court and it's the other way around if they are co-perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So the military court will only have jurisdiction to try them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, jurisdiction will be in the hands of the military court if they are co-perpetrators, if they are accessories, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And what happens in the case of a civilian perpetrator joining with a VJ perpetrator, both join to commit a crime, then what happens? Is the same position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is the same, but the word order is different. Did the civilian commit the crime with the military person or did the military person commit a crime with the civilian? The answer is one and the same. If the civilian and military person committed a crime as co-perpetrators and if the military person is to be tried by the military court, then that same court is going to try the other person as well, the civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I must say, I find this very confusing, Mr. Radosavljevic. There must be simpler ways of explaining this. If two courts on the face of it have jurisdiction, does one have priority over the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, it is not two courts that have jurisdiction. The Law on Military Courts is lex specialis, and it prescribes the solution that I refer to, that if these two persons commit a crime together and if the military person is to be tried by a military court, then automatically the military court takes over that case for the civilian co-perpetrator, too. I think that that is perfectly clear. There is nothing unclear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just one small matter, page 39, 14, the judgement becomes final, not valid, 39, 14. I didn't want to interrupt the Judges while you were posing questions, and that's in the transcript, 39, 14. It says: "Until the judgement becomes valid." The witness says: "Until the judgement becomes final" after the appeal court decides on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I will ask CLSS to check that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes, that is correct. Interpreter's correction: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It has been corrected. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, in paragraph 23 of your statement you say that: "The Law on Criminal Proceedings specifically states that if there are reasonable grounds to suspect that there is a crime for which the Prosecutor must act ex officio, then Internal Affairs have a duty to undertake measures to find the perpetrator, to prevent him from escaping ... secure the scene," et cetera. Can you explain to me what that means, what the prosecutor is acting ex officio?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The law prescribes what crimes are dealt with ex officio and in which cases charges are brought by private person. It is not for our assessment, but it is the law that specifically says that for such and such a crime there are indictments issued ex officio and for others a person, individual person, can bring charges. So it is only for some crimes that charges are brought ex officio, or rather, in most cases it is the prosecutor who has the official duty to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement there when you're talking about internal affairs, you mean the personnel from the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the police, the MUP, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. In the last paragraph of your statement you mention Exhibit 4D171, and I can hand you a hard copy of that exhibit. You say this is a document that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 6th of April, 2001, in a report to the 3rd Army commander about criminal proceedings. You mentioned that there were investigations pending against 47 persons for crimes resulting in death or threat to human life and limb, and six -- well, six of the 47 were for crimes resulting in death or threat to life and limb. One of those individuals was Colonel Stosic. We've heard some evidence about his case here. Can you tell us what you know about the outcome of the proceedings, if any, that arose from the investigation into his involvement. At this time, in 2001, it indicates it was suspended due to lack of evidence. Was that the final outcome?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think that was the case. Believe me, I'm not quite sure, I'm not making an assertion, but I think that nothing changed after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And a little further on, I'm not sure what page it is in the B/C/S, you mention that indictments against 182 persons include 13 persons charged with crimes resulting in death or other consequences related to human life and limb. And you mention the following persons, but I see only ten names listed. Was that intentional just to list the ten? Were the other three left out by oversight? Or do you know? Do you find that? The first person listed is Major Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I see that, yes. I see that there is an addition here under number 10 Bozidar Sudarski. Yes, it is correct that this information should have been contained. This is probably an omission, probably, I'm saying probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So do you know who the other three individuals against whom indictments were returned for crimes resulting in death?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. If you could jog my memory, perhaps I could say a bit more. I don't know what person this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know either. It's your report that says there were 13 persons charged with crimes and only list ten. I wonder if you could help us out as to who the other three might be?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I yes, that's what you mean. I beg your pardon, I beg your pardon. Now I understand from the text here. It says here that out of these 13 persons ten are threats to human life and limb and then ten, or rather, nine are referred to, the tenth one is missing. And there are three other persons that are referred to in this report, but not with regard to crimes with regards to human life and limb but rapes are the crimes involved in this other case and they are described here, what it is that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see following on that there are four persons charged with crimes against personal dignity, so that would make 14 instead of 13. Can you explain that difference?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Let's go back to this again. Then it's all right. There is no mistake in what I said, 13 persons is the total. Nine against life and limb and four for rape, crimes of rape, nine plus four is 13, but I certainly omitted Sudarski, that would be a total of 14. That's what I missed. So ten would be against life and limb and three for, or rather, four for rape. But the problem is that this one person was omitted, so the result was not 14 but the only 13. That's the only discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the last page in English, and I'm not sure if it's on your last page, but three paragraphs above the signature block it mentions -- it mentions three incidents of multiple murder. One of those was -- the third incident relates to the discovery of 144 fresh graves in Izbica village sector on 29 May 1999. It said: "The files do not contain any reliable evidence on the circumstances in which these persons were killed." Is that correct? In April 2001 the files didn't have any reliable evidence about how some of the 144 people found in Izbica village were killed? Hadn't autopsies been done?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course there was no evidence pointing that, absolutely, and I believe that is why the case was deferred. I haven't found it yet in this document, but I remember -- I seem to remember that the case was deferred. Could you please help me in this -- Ah, yes, I see. One incident relates to the discovery of -- Ah, I see. All right. Right. It's not written here, but as far as I can remember I deferred that case. The case was referred, it didn't remain in the military court in Nis, it was deferred to the civilian prosecutor in charge in order to pursue the matter. Until then, I did not have any elements as to how it was that these persons had lost their lives, and I particularly did not have any evidence indicating that the military was responsible for their deaths. So that is why I referred the case to the civilian jurisdiction, but I think that by then it hadn't been decided yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you about one last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give us a date for the reference of the case to the civilian prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you just now I think I referred it. I don't know the date, but if that did happen, if I said this right, it must have been after this date, after the date of this information. I really do not know when this took place, probably after 2001, perhaps 2003, 2004. It certainly didn't take place immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That can be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, were you aware of General Pavkovic having some role in organizing exhumations and autopsies of bodies from that mass grave in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Aleksic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask my learned friend Mr. Hannis to give us a transcript reference and where this reference to Izbica comes from. Since we have other evidence, perhaps it would be good to discuss this when the witness is out of the courtroom. So perhaps he could be asked to leave the courtroom. I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Hannis, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
