utterances.text: No reason for any interruption here. Please continue, Mr. Hannis. Your question's straightforward and doesn't depend on anything in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, do I need to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of General Pavkovic having had some role in organizing exhumations and autopsies of bodies from those graves in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any such thing, absolutely. Izbica is in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija I think and there were first-instance military prosecutors who was in charge there, and at that time I didn't know anything about their work, I mean I did not know whether they were in contact with him from that point of view. But after the war, I mean until the present day, I haven't heard anything about this, about him having done anything in that sense. But I know it's only the investigating judge who can order an exhumation and nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you one last question. You mentioned a person you'd talked to before, I think you mentioned the name of Zlatan Mancic, I think you said he's a client of yours now. I would ask you to look at Exhibit P962. This is a list of filed criminal reports against perpetrators in the 549th Motorised Brigade for crimes between May 1998 and July 1999. I can hand you the hard copy and ask you to look at the entry for item number 103 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a correction, I think Mr. Hannis misspoke. The witness had said that he was a witness in a case that he was dealing with as a private lawyer, not that he was a client of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is correct, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, isn't it, sir, you said he was a witness, not a client?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you find item number 103 on that list? It's page 27 of the English.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It states Zlatan Mancic who was a major and the crime was war crime against civilians and it indicated a seven-year imprisonment changed to 14 years. We had evidence from another witness who testified in closed session about this and indicated that that sentence of 14 years must have been reduced because the individual was no longer in prison and that he had been promoted at some point during the proceedings to colonel. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was promoted to the rank of colonel, but I don't think so. I have absolutely never heard of that, of him being a colonel. For us, he was always Lieutenant-Colonel Zlatan Mancic. I am sorry, did the question go beyond that? Maybe I did not hear everything you asked me. Was your question only whether he was a colonel or not or did it go beyond that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, here on the report he's listed as a major, and we had a witness indicate that he knew him as a colonel. So I had wondered whether he had been promoted during the proceedings against him for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: If that was the case, but I'm not sure of that but it is possible, that he certainly wasn't promoted during the criminal proceedings. Indeed, I may be making a mistake if I say this, but I seem to remember that the prosecutor's office, the peacetime prosecutor's office after the war asked for some information concerning him and that it was only then that they realised that he had committed a crime and that he was processed later. And then perhaps he was promoted before that, but this is just something that I am remembering now. It is possible that that was not actually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And what kind of case is he a witness in now, if you know?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: He's a witness before the district court in Pirot against Boban Stancic, a civilian who is being prosecuted for abuse of official capacity. This has nothing to do with the military or the war; it has to do with something that happened in civilian life last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few matters by way of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radosavljevic, would you tell the Court, first of all, whether there's a distinction in our legal system between delivering an indictment and the expression that an indictment has legally entered into force?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a distinction and it is reflected in the following: An indictment enters into legal force when it has been served and when the deadline for objection has expired without any objection being filed. It is not enough to serve the indictment. It also has to enter into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And what is the deadline for objection?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the last subject you discussed with my learned friend Mr. Hannis, this witness Mancic, you said the peacetime prosecutor's office asked for additional information, which one?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: The military prosecutor in Nis, the prosecutor's office where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. You said there were no pressures exerted. Just tell the Trial Chamber, did commanders along the chain of command, such as Generals Pavkovic or Lazarevic, were they able to issue you prosecutors with any instructions how to act in specific cases, whether to prosecute, whether to initiate proceedings, or to abandon the case?

utterances.speaker: STANIMIR RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: They were absolutely not able to do that under the law and they never tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Radosavljevic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence and to assist us. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next is Zarko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Aleksic on behalf of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Aleksic. Where are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can we have your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Zarko Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the 28th of September this year, did you give a statement to the Defence team of General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to read that statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If the same questions were put to you today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Exhibit 4D502, and I should like to tender this exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the number of the previous statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour, I'm a bit tired. 4D501.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you very, very briefly tell the Trial Chamber about your military career and the positions you occupied at various times.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: After my initial duties as commanding officer in the 203rd Artillery Brigade, I completed the higher military political school in Belgrade, after which I was assigned to another duty at the command of the Pristina Corps at the department for information and morale. Since I had a degree in journalism, I was assigned to public relations. My service in the command of the Pristina Corps enabled me to get more familiar with the overall situation in Kosovo and Metohija, especially the real history of Serb-Albanian relations over the past hundred or so years. After this position, I was transferred to the command of the 3rd Army to become assistant chief for combat training, and later on I became chief of the department for training. I stayed in that position until 2000, when I was appointed assistant commander for the 3rd Army for information and morale and remained there until my retirement in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. So in 1998 you were in which position?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I was chief of the section for training at the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1998 and exactly when did you spend any time at the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In that year, from end July until end August, I was on the forward command post of the 3rd Army command in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber which particular duties you performed there during your stint at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: At the forward command post I continued to perform my usual duties as prescribed by the establishment, that is, the normal duties of the chief of division for military training, according to the plan and programme for that month. I also performed some duties at the army command, mainly operations duties, and we had special work to do concerning reporting to commanders at the forward command post and informing [as interpreted] the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: During your stay at the forward command post, did you participate in the development of combat orders, development of plans, decisions on the use of units, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That kind of tasks were handled usually by officers from the division for combat-readiness and operations from the command of the 3rd Army because that was their job according to the establishment, but I was familiar with those assignments. However, it was their main duty. My main duty was as chief of the division for military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I believe on page 53, line 21, the witness said the decision of the commander of the Pristina Corps was approved, approved, instead of informing. Can I clarify this with the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you say -- Colonel, could you say again at the forward command post did you say that the decision of the commander of the 3rd Army as developed by the Pristina Corps was approved?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The forward command post, the decision of the commander of the Pristina Corps was approved by the commander of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement -- strike that. As far as 1999 is concerned, can you just tell us briefly, after the state of war was proclaimed, what were your primary tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: After the state of war was proclaimed, I worked as chief of division for military training in the command of the 3rd Army, and after that on the orders of the commander of the 3rd Army I was assigned to become commander of the collection -- sorry, reception centre, a centre receiving volunteers, providing training, and assigning personnel to units of the 3rd Army. I stayed in that position until the middle of May, after which I performed other duties at the command of the 3rd Army on the orders of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In this work that you performed, and you said you were in charge of receiving volunteers, were there any problems, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Initially, in the initial period, there were problems and the problems were mainly in the reception centre of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this exhibit is mentioned in the statement we will briefly deal with it. Can we call in e-court, please, P1938.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did you see this document and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I recognise the document. I wrote it. It was signed by the commander of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just tell the Trial Chamber briefly about the contents.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: By virtue of this document, the command of the 3rd Army addresses itself to the supreme staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and presents a number of problems in the work of the reception centre of the 1st Army and also requests from the Supreme Command that measures be taken to redress the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Did it happen? Is it the case that two or three days later a new order from the Supreme Command Staff arrived?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's correct. A new order arrived from the Supreme Command Staff, and after that the problems did not recur.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up in e-court 4D353.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: This order had to do with the command of the 3rd Army to the effect that wartime units cannot accept volunteers into their units bypassing the reception centre of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any Defence counsel with questions? Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good afternoon, my name is Djuro Cepic. I appear here for General Lazarevic, and I have a few questions for you. ?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of your statement I find a description of the location where training was performed within the 3rd Army, you said Zajecar, Pirot, Nis, and you named the duration. I would like to know, how long was military training in the centres in Pozarevac and Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In the military training centres of Pozarevac and Valjevo, combat training for soldiers was two months and 20 days. In those centres after that, they would be transferred to army units on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where their combat training continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let us be more precise. From those centres, Pozarevac and Valjevo, could the soldiers be sent to any unit on the territory of the then-FR Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: They could be sent to any units of the then-Army of Yugoslavia. Their transfer was handled by a special commission of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia through computer systems to avoid any kind of personal requests and such, requests by parents, commanding officers, and similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a few questions for this witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic and I am here for Sreten Lukic before this Court. I would like your assistance in trying to understand certain aspects that remained unclear. I will be dealing with paragraphs of your statement, 23, 24, and 25. Let us begin with para 23 where you say that the 3rd Army command received reports from the Pristina Corps and other subordinated units regularly at the forward command post, and based on the received information we made our own combat report that we sent daily to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army so that they had complete daily information as well. One copy of the report would be sent to the command of the 3rd Army in Nis for their information. I would like to ask you, this is a regular kind of reporting within the Army of Yugoslavia in both 1998 and 1999, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 6D1310. We do not have a translation for this document, but we will only be using a small passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, who is it that sends this combat report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who is the combat report being sent to?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: To the command of the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command Staff and the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from when is it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The 17th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 3 on e-court, page 3 of this document, at the bottom of the page, number 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please be so kind as to read this paragraph out to us, number 8, the second bullet point.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "Implementing the activity of searching the terrain in concert with the MUP of Serbia in the areas or regions of the Rugovo Gorge, Zlaz, and Drenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it has to do partly with Rugovska Klisura, the gorge of Rugovo. We would like to focus on that.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Can I have a look again? What's the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to see on e-court 5D215, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure the transcript reflects the answer there about the date. What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in this document that is on the screen now, 5D215, tell me if this is correct. Again what is being sent is a combat report by the command of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This report is a day later, the 18th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see paragraph 2, the lower part of the page, please. So number 2, situation and activities of units of the Pristina Corps, 2.1, activity, effects, consequences, and the rest. We have the second paragraph too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it. It begins with the words: "Action has started ..."

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "Action as started in concert with the MUP of Serbia in searching the area, breaking up and destroying the Siptar terrorist forces in the regions of Rugovska Klisura, Drenica, and Zlaz. Action is also underway and in accordance with the reports of subordinates they are taking place according to plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view from these documents dated the 17th and the 18th of April, can one see that parts of the Pristina Corps were engaged in searching the terrain and actively participated in destroying the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what's written in these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We also see that these activities are taking place according to plan?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That is what is stated in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you a third document, 4D420. We have the upper part on our screens now, that's what we need. Can you tell us who's sending this report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To who?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: To the Supreme Command Staff to the head personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The 20th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you now please be so kind as to read the beginning of the document after paragraph number 1.3, paragraphs that start with bullet points. It says: "At the meeting of the Supreme Command Staff ..."

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "At the meeting of the Supreme Command Staff on the 12th of April," and I cannot see the year, is it legible in your copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see the 12th of April, 1999, and the English translation says 1999; however, if you do not see you can go on.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "The supreme commander of the FRY issued a precise task with regard to breaking up the remaining groups of STS and regulated that in the next seven days only the JSO and SAJ of the MUP of Serbia were to be engaged in the execution of these tasks."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next bullet point.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "In this operation the following VJ units were to be engaged in the blockade: The 2nd Battalion of the 58th lpbr, the 1st and 2nd kag engaged in the blockade of the general area of Rugovska Klisura and were not engaged in taking active part. That is why we could not halt the said operation because it was planned and organized by the competent MUP command."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw in your statement that you say and that you describe the way in which information was conveyed to the 3rd Army and by the 3rd Army. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand what you're saying, to the 3rd Army and by the 3rd Army? What?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page, or rather, paragraph 23 of your statement you say: "The 3rd Army command received regular reports on a regular basis from Pristina Corps and other subunits who were also preparing our military reports based on gathered information sent them to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army on daily basis in order to inform them." Now I would like to ask you the following. In this area that was under the control of the Pristina Corps, are there some other units of the Army of Yugoslavia that are outside the Pristina Corps and that were not within it and that were not resubordinated to it? Do you know about any such thing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: You're asking about 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: At this time I was in the command of the 3rd Army and I was commander of the reception centre for receiving volunteers; therefore, I'm not aware what was going on then in the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In your view, as a soldier could anybody else report from the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps on behalf of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I am an expert for training and combat-readiness, not for command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you give us any kind of explanation how it came to be that these two commands report in different ways about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I cannot engage in guess-work and make comments with regard to such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on. Now I would like to ask you something in relation to paragraph 24 of your statement. Paragraph 24, you say the following. "During 1998 the basic tasks of the Army of Yugoslavia were securing the country border, both in-depth and in line, securing the military facilities of special importance, securing the army forces in Kosovo and Metohija, providing communication information from terrorist forces and providing support to the MUP forces in blocking specific targets, and in providing fire support."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have on e-court 4D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D97. Could we see page 3 of this document straight away. We just need the very bottom of the page with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we see here that you took the minutes?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 1 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please help us on this. According to these minute, who is it that is reporting here and could you please help us with the abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Minutes from the briefing of the command -- briefing of the commander of the Pristina Corps, the command of the military district of Pristina, and the 202nd logistics base, and the command --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you read that too quickly for the interpreter. Could you read it again, please, and a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, these are minutes from the briefing of the commander of the Pristina Corps, the commander of the military district of Pristina, and the commander of the 202nd logistics base, as well as the organs of the command of the 3rd Army at the forward command post on the 7th of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Towards the top of the page it says: "Colonel Djakovic" and the first bullet point states the following: "We have drafted a decision on crushing the DTS in the Glodjane village area." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page it's the commander who is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who's the commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Army, General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the bottom of the page eight lines from the bottom of the page or three lines up from the bottom on the English, in the English version, the commander says: "I adopt the decision of the commander of the Pristina Corps to destroy the DTS in the village of Glodjane." At this point in time there is already a decision on destroying the terrorists -- crushing the terrorists in the village of Glodjane; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The sixth line from the top. In English it's page 2, the second separate paragraph, line 3, that says: "For us ..." The commander says: "For us it is important to capture territory, and later on we will pursue the next targets. Thus, we will have completed the task from the president of the FRY." My question is and in relation to that I'm going to show you another document later on: Do you know and can we agree that this is a task that is contained in the plan that was approved by the president of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That is what is derived from this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The third paragraph in English and in Serbian it says: "Colonel Djakovic explained the disposition of forces in Metohija and Drenica, Mount Cicavica, Bajgora, and Rugovska Klisura," and so on and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So over here there is a reference to Rugovska Klisura again, right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the next line -- oh, yes, and this has to do with Colonel Djakovic and it's the same in the English version. "The disposition of BG," meaning combat groups, right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "He is giving a more detailed explanation on the map," it has to do with the disposition of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And all of it is already marked on the map, right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Five lines below that, also in the English version, in parenthesis it says: "He explained the disposition of MUP forces in more detail on the map," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what is marked on the map are the MUP forces, too, right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's the way it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next line further down in English it says: "NS" with a diacritic, that is the Chief of Staff, right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Chief of Staff says: "Given the positions of the state and military leadership, the terminology we shall use is 'supporting MUP forces.'" My question is: Is it correct that this term was used in the future every time when the Army of Yugoslavia was in action, combat action, against terrorists with the MUP units?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: This term was used most often at the forward command post of the 3rd Army when actions against the terrorists were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Four lines down further, also in English, again it's the commander who has the floor and in the document it says that he said: "We will have to make a separate plan for each engagement -- for each segment of engagement of forces." Was this actually carried out in future actions, Colonel? Was a separate plan made for each action? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It's been a long time since then, and also this is not my very own specialty that I would know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thought that since you kept the minutes, whether in the future perhaps you kept minutes again and you knew about it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did not take minutes every day, only when ordered, because there were about ten other officers at the forward command post of the 3rd Army who did the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever attend a meeting where a plan was made?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Which meeting do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any meeting where a plan was made to conduct anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: At the forward command post of the 3rd Army command plans were not made, they were only approved there. Plans were made at the corps command and the corps commander was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next line also in English says: "In future, we will have to send the MUP precise tasks." Later on, after that, did you see a plan at the forward command post, including tasks for the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see a map where MUP units were drawn in or, more precisely, PJP units?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I did not see a map where MUP or PJP units would be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next line. "For every segment we have to make a separate plan for the destruction of staffs of terrorists." Are you aware if separate plans were made?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Colonel Djakovic said that, but I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know about a five-stage plan to combat terrorism?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to move on to paragraph 25 of your statement where you say: "I know that our units blocked the villages of Junik and Jasic on the orders of the 3rd Army command. I also know that MUP support was given to for the villages: Balabac, Prilep, and Glodjane. The aim of this action was to provide communication on the roads. It was secured by the disposition, by the deployment in important facilities near the communication lines made by the battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think there might be a translation issue with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- The English translation we have and what was just quoted. Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a battalion in the transcript. It was done by deploying combat groups at prominent features near roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is going to be your question on this, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question should be regarding the role of the participants in this action because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could we -- if there is doubt about the translation, could you please, first of all, have the witness slowly read paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up on e-court 4D501, paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Our English version of this statement differs significantly from the original we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, would you please read out aloud paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "I know that our units carried out the blockade of villages Junik and Jasic pursuant to orders of the 3rd Army command. I also know that MUP forces provided support also around villages Balabac, Prilep, and Glodjane. The purpose of the action was to secure communication along roads which was done by deploying combat groups at prominent features near the roads."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us not go too broadly. I'll take as example Junik and Jasic villages and ask you about the involvement of army units in this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we first call up in e-court 4D119.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, tell me, who is sending the report to whom and on what date?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Army, date 22nd July, 1998, to the command of the Pristina Corps, to the commander personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the sentence that begins with: "Since ..."

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "Since the president of the SRY approved the second-stage plan on the 21st of July, 1998 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's enough. So we see that it is a plan in several stages and was approved by the president of the SRY on the 21st of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that the plan approved by the FRY president served as a basis for performing these actions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: We can conclude that from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up on e-court 6D1318.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can we see who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: The command of the Pristina Corps from the forward command post 24 July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible, because you say you don't know about a five-stage plan, I'm asking is it possible that this is an elaboration of the plan approved by the FRY president three days earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Please, sir, at this time I was in the command of the 3rd Army. It was the month of July. I was not at the forward command post. Second, all these documents that you have enumerated so far belong in the remit of the department for operations and combat-readiness. I can only confirm that what is written is written. I am not the kind of witness who can interpret these documents that were made by others, others who know these things better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this, but in your statement, paragraph 25, you spoke precisely about this.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: In that statement I said I was aware, which doesn't mean that I had complete knowledge of the situation like the corps commander or somebody else from the 3rd Army commander had, somebody who had daily contact with these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we finalise this quickly. Do you allow the possibility that you were not sufficiently aware and sufficiently familiar and that what you said in paragraph 25 is not actually true, so that the army units of Yugoslavia had an active role rather than only a supporting one? If you don't accept my proposition, we will have to go through more documents and further down this document.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you allow the possibility that the information accessible to you at the moment when you gave this statement, when you spoke about the role of the VJ and MUP in the battle for Junik is not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that during the time when I was at the forward command post of the 3rd Army command actions were going on against terrorists in the said locations, and these actions involved forces of the Pristina Corps and forces of the MUP. That much I know. What their precise tasks were, I cannot testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Thank you for answering my questions. I have no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Kostic, we have to have a break at this stage for about half an hour. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher while we have that break and we'll see you again at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stamp, the Prosecutor. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I start by asking you a couple of things about your role, as indicated in your statement, and perhaps it would be easier if I hand to you with the assistance of the usher a copy of your statement in your language. And if we could look at paragraphs 22 and paragraphs 26, and what I'm really interested in is what role you played. The first sentence of paragraph 2 is sufficient and if you could look at the first sentence of paragraph 26. Firstly, in paragraph 22 are you referring to the forward command post, which you say was in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor. I'm talking about the forward command post that was in Pristina in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 26 you also refer to the forward command post in Kursumlija.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Correct, sir, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So can you explain that. Did the forward command post move from one place to another or maybe I should start by asking you: When you refer in paragraph 26 to the forward command post in Kursumlija, when are you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Those are events just before the aggression against our country started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the forward command post had been in Pristina, and shortly before the -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: No, no. As for paragraph 26, that relates to the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Kursumlija, and that is the period of 1999 just before the aggression started, the aggression of the NATO forces against our country. That's when the forward command post of the 3rd Army was formed in Kursumlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, it seems to me that this is saying that you took over command of the forward command post in Kursumlija from General Stojimirovic. Is my understanding of that first sentence correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: General Stojimirovic was the most senior commanding officer at the forward command post in Kursumlija, but in his absence I stood in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, what was the role of the most senior officer at the forward command post in Kursumlija?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Those were events just before the start of the NATO aggression against our country when numerous tasks of the 3rd Army units were being dealt with related to our preparations for defence against aggression. From that forward command post there was a better insight into the situation within units and measures were taken for all planned tasks as ordered by the 3rd Army commander to be implemented as efficiently and as successfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what was your role when you took over as the most senior person there, what did you do in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: We were following the status of units at the 3rd Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just want to know what you did, what was your function when you took over in the absence of General Stojimirovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Sir, I did not take over the duties of General Stojimirovic, I just stood in for him when he was temporarily absent from the forward command post. That's what I stated in my written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And how --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: And his absences were usually not longer than one day, and that was when on orders of the army commander he had to leave the forward command post and deal with other duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I ask you a couple questions about paragraph 8 of your statement, and I'm moving on to something else, training of soldiers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, can I be clear about one thing, and it may sound a silly question to you, Mr. Kostic. But can an army such as the 3rd Army at any given time have more than one forward command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, Mr. President, in the period from 1999 the 3rd Army command had only one forward command post, and that was in Kursumlija. If you mean 1998, the events were different and the forward command post was in Pristina. So the command of the 3rd Army did not simultaneously have two forward command posts, just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said at paragraph 8 that training of soldiers that are in military service is obtained at basic units and training centres and lasted five months and 20 days, which is at the end of the military service. The soldiers on military service, are they personnel referred to as conscripts or am I using that term wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: All of them were military conscripts, but these ones were recruits who were doing their regular, compulsory military service. Those who had already completed their military service continue always to be conscripts, and they have a -- wartime assignments in one of the units of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on to paragraph 41. In that paragraph you speak of inspections that you conducted -- but firstly, how many inspections did you conduct after the middle of May 1999, during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Sir, after the said period I performed one inspection in the 354th Brigade of the Pristina Corps. I led up to ten colonels on that inspection and the inspection itself took ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate dates of the inspection?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember who accompanied you on that inspection?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: On the team that I led there were chief of infantry, Colonel Milojkovic; from the logistics, Colonel Vidojkovic; and other commanding officers I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And your finding was that in all but one battalion discipline was at a high level?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Correct, sir. In some battalions it was at a very high level, that is, a very high level of combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you a document and explain you to explain one or two things to me, it's 5D436. This is a report signed by Lieutenant-General Terzic about a tour of inspection of the 354th Infantry Brigade and it's sent to the team leader, Colonel-General Velickovic. Is -- does that indicate that this is the same inspection that you were a part of, it's dated the 29th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It's not the same inspection tour. It was a different inspection tour by the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it seemed -- it seems from this to have taken place just about the same time as yours. This is dated the 27th of May, and you I think indicate that yours was after the middle of May, 1999. Would this document be referring to an inspection which took place at about the same time as yours?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the time, the exact time, when I led that inspection to that brigade, and I was not aware that another team from the General Staff this time also carried out an inspection in the same brigade. I'm seeing this document for the very first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, you say that this was the only inspection you carried out. Was there any particular reason for an inspection of that brigade to be ordered? Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I know that there was a reason in one of the battalions. In this brigade there were incidents of indiscipline and other problems, and that's when the army commander ordered that an inspection team be formed, that it should go to that brigade to assist the brigade command and all other units to resolve those problems. We spent several days in that brigade until we redressed the situation in that unit and brought it to the required level so that it could be used again for its purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at page 2 of the document in front of you and it's also page 2 in English under the subheading: "Abandonment of posts." This inspection seems to have found in the first paragraph under the heading: "2. Abandonment of posts," that in the 3rd Infantry Battalion on the 21st of May, a total of 350 men, including 12 officers, abandoned their positions. Is this the battalion you were speaking about that you said was the only one that had disciplinary problems, the 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the second and third paragraphs under that same rubric you will see that the same report is made in respect to indiscipline or abandonment of positions in respect to the 1st Infantry Brigade in the second paragraph, 750 men abandoned their positions; in the third paragraph in respect to the 100-millimetre [sic] Howitzer Battalion one part of that battalion left their position. Did you not find that there were disciplinary problems in these battalions as well as was apparently was found by the inspectors from the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: From this document I conclude that this inspection from the Supreme Command Staff preceded the inspection by the team from the 3rd Army command, and the team of the 3rd Army command inspected this unit much later when the situation had been improved and resolved in that part of the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the record, Mr. Stamp read this abbreviation as 1st Infantry Brigade, page 77, line 23. It should be the 1st Infantry Battalion, to avoid misunderstanding later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In any case, what I'd really like you to explain is what does it mean when it is said that 120 men abandoned their positions, is there a distinction between that and desertion?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: There is a difference, sir. Those people who abandoned their positions were later, after certain steps were taken, returned to their units and continued to serve. Those who deserted were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mean those who deserted evinced an intention to abandon their positions permanently? Is that a correct understanding of the distinction?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at the three paragraphs here you will see that in respect to 150 men in the first paragraph, 750 men in the second paragraph, and an unascertained amount of men in the third paragraph relating to the 105th Howitzer Battalion, you will see that they were returned -- well, it says: "The brigade commander returned the men to the battalion on the 21st of May -- 24th of May." In the second paragraph: "The brigade commander collected the weapons and military equipment from the deserters and organized their return to the combat area on the 24th of May." Were -- what I'm trying to understand is these men abandoned their positions as a group and go somewhere and were collected as a group and returned to the positions they should have been in.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: When they abandoned their positions, I did not witness it. But I was a witness when they were returned to their units because I was in the process together with General Stojimirovic at the mobilisation assembly point. We worked with those people, we had their requests, and the army took steps to meet reasonable requests; to the extent possible those people were given three to seven days home leave. And after that leave they came back to the mobilisation and assembly point of their own accord and were returned to the units of the 354th Motorised Brigade in an organized way. Their return, therefore, was organized, but how exactly they went absent without official leave I cannot tell you. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that these were large groups of men, and that's only an observation I make. And when I look at the second paragraph in that heading I see that the brigade commander collected weapons and equipment and organized their return. Do you know if these men abandoned their positions with their weapons, because that seems to be indicated here?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: It follows from this that they went AWAL with their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not there were any investigations on their return as to what they were doing and where they were with these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Could you let me read this passage again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "Area of the mobilisation assembly point, the brigade commander assembled the personnel that had abandoned their positions and organized their return to the combat deployment area for 27th May." This sentence makes no sentence. He collected their weapons and military equipment from the deserters, that is, and organized their return. How did he organize their return without their weapons and equipment? That's what this seems to be saying. I cannot testify about this. I was not there and I do not know anything about it. I'm seeing this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: And this sentence I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Well, take your eyes off the document for a bit. After the return of these large groups of apparently heavily armed men in the context of Kosovo, do you know if there was any investigation on their return about where they were and what they were doing with these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, I really would be interested in the basis for this kind of question. Heavily armed men, what is the basis for this kind of wording?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I said apparently heavily armed because to a civilian like myself a soldier armed with military equipment is heavily armed, but then "heavily" is probably a violent term. I withdraw the word heavily and just say armed men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any investigations after return of these large groups of armed soldiers as to where they were and what they were doing during the time when they abandoned their posts?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that is known to the command of the brigade, the corps command, and the command of the 3rd Army. These persons left their positions and went to the mobilisation point in Kursumlija. That is their place of residence. That is where they got a few days of leave to resolve the problems that they had pointed out. For the most part these were problems related to their very living and to financial matters. Most of them returned to the assembly point on orders of the brigade commander, and they were returned in an organized fashion to the position; that is to say in relation to this personnel that returned to the mobilisation assembly point in an organized fashion and was taken to the positions of the 354th Brigade in an organized fashion as well. No disciplinary measures were taken, and they were not held responsible. Measures were taken against certain officers in these battalions, meaning that some officers were dismissed and others were appointed, more responsible ones, because they, these officers, bore part of the responsibility for that kind of a situation, or rather, most of the responsibility for that kind of a situation. Now, what other kinds of measures were taken in respect of criminal prosecution, et cetera, I am not in a position to answer now because I don't know, or rather, it's been quite a while since then and I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sounds more like going on strike than deserting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this personnel had been on their positions for over two months under very difficult conditions of combat operations. People were fed up. They were too strained. They couldn't take it at a certain point, and what happened happened. There were some omissions on the part of the brigade command that did not organize leaves of absence and family visits for soldiers and officers on time. This was too much of a burden for the soldiers and officers, and in addition to that there were losses in these units. All of this had an influence on the state of morale in these units, so what happened is what we've been discussing now. Further on, the brigade command worked better and the battalion commanders, too. So these problems were eliminated later on and up until the end of the war the command of the brigade and the brigade successfully carried out all their combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what you've told us is that when they abandoned their posts they went to the barracks, which is not desertion in the ordinary sense. It's something odd, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not say that they went to barracks. I said that they went to the mobilisation assembly point, and that is not one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, equally strange to go to the mobilisation assembly point, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, mobilisation assembly point, or rather, this mobilisation assembly point is in Kursumlija where the barracks of this brigade is, too, that is where their native villages are as well. So that was the basic motive why they had abandoned their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did they stay with the army by going to a mobilisation assembly point or barracks or did they go home or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They remained at the mobilisation assembly point. That is where the brigade command was. I came there with General Ljubisa Stojimirovic. We talked to the men there in an organized manner. They pointed out certain requests and certain problems. General Ljubisa Stojimirovic decided as deputy army commander to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to go into the detail of what was discussed. It's the location of these men and where they went that's the issue for Mr. Stamp. We've heard evidence, some evidence of members of the army being dissatisfied with their pay and conditions when compared with those of the MUP. Is this an example of that or is this quite unrelated to that phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not aware of what kind of salaries members of the MUP had, whether they received them regularly or not. As far as I can see things viewed from this time distance as well, these are problems, family problems. And for the most part they pertain to problems of a financial nature. People pointed out that they had quite a few such problems that in companies they were not receiving salaries and they referred to other reasons, too, why it was that they had abandoned positions. One of these other reasons was that they asked to be replaced by other reservists who did not have war assignments among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But just to be sure we're talking about the same thing. You're talking about the situation that you observed when you went there sometime long after the 27th of May, which is the date of the document I just showed you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: If I understood your question, Mr. Prosecutor, you are referring to this situation when with General Stojimirovic and other officers from the 3rd Army I went to the mobilisation assembly point in Kursumlija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I was referring to the findings of the team of inspectors in the document dated the 27th of May that I just showed you when this referred to significant abandonment of posts in three battalions. I think you are saying that was supposed to have happened a long time before you actually went to that brigade. Am I correct in understanding it that way?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: When these units abandoned positions and came to the mobilisation assembly point in Kursumlija, I with General Stojimirovic and other officers talked to them at this mobilisation assembly point. That happened then. Considerably after this event I led an inspection, when these personnel returned to positions. So these are two separate points in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So therefore you have some personal knowledge about the matters discussed in the document, in the report, that is in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I know when this abandonment of positions happened and when the units returned to the mobilisation assembly point because I was present then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by considerably after this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I led a team of the command of the 3rd Army to tour this brigade and inspect it when all units and personnel had returned to the brigade. That is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "Considerably" is what I'm referring to. What does that mean, "considerably after"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot remember exactly when this inspection took place, the one that I led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Roughly how long after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, roughly about ten days, ten to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The war would be over in about 15 days, so was it right at the very end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was towards the end, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At paragraphs 33, 34 of your statement, if you have a quick look there, please, the last sentence of paragraph 33: "The regulations did not allow for special volunteer units to be created and the majority of volunteers behaved with discipline in the war units." Firstly -- well, before I ask you these questions. Can I -- you said when you were asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think that there is a problem with the translation. It says "should." Could the witness read out that paragraph in his own language. That would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you say is the problem with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the original, Your Honour, it says: "According to regulations they were supposed to be according to their specialties VES," I must be tired, but it says here in line 15, it says "special volunteer units," it's not special volunteer units. What is referred to is their military evidentiary specialty, what they had been trained for, their VES.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, would you read the last sentence of paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President: "According to the rules they were supposed to be deployed according" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please, the last sentence, the last sentence of paragraph 33. There only is one in B/C/S, is there, okay. Please read the whole of paragraph 33.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat. "According to the rules they were supposed to be deployed according to their specialties VES and to be sent four to five respectively per unit and not to have separate volunteer units established."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's exactly what it says at the moment, Mr. Aleksic. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you also go on to say in paragraph 34: "The volunteers or the majority of volunteers behaved with discipline in war units." And what I was saying before Mr. Aleksic intervened is that before I proceed to ask you questions about those statements, I noted that you said in answer to him or perhaps in answer to Mr. Lukic, perhaps, that in 1999 you were in the reception centre and therefore you were not aware of what was going on in the zone of responsibility of the Pristina Corps. So if that which you said today is correct, how would you be aware that the majority of volunteers behaved with discipline in the war units?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this assessment of mine is based on analyses that we conducted immediately after the war in commands of corps and brigades, or rather, at the level of the 3rd Army. Many analyses of combat-readiness were carried out, and a lot of experience was drawn from combat activities. We sublimated all of that, processed all of that, and from these analyses and reports I know how volunteers behaved. These volunteers who were returned, about 60 are referred to here, were returned to the reception centre of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "behaved with discipline," you are just speaking about their conduct in -- withdrawn. We have before the Court evidence of complaints being raised from various quarters, in particular from the MUP, about the misconduct of VJ units - and I stress the word units - of volunteers. Did you ever hear about those reports? Maybe I should read you one. Time is going -- I won't show you this. This is P1996 at page 5 of the English at a 7th of May meeting of the MUP staff, the chief of the Pristina MUP indicated that: "The military is not taking sufficient measures and most crimes are being perpetrated by VJ members. Volunteer units with VJ uniforms must be disbanded." Were you aware of these types of complaints about undisciplined behaviour or criminal conduct by volunteer or volunteer units during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this report of the MUP that you are referring to now is something I hear of for the first time right now, that is to say that I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Secondly, there is an order of the command of the 3rd Army that volunteers be deployed in wartime units according to their specialties, that is to say not to have compact units because as such they are not capable of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question, and that is that you were not aware of the complaint. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you or were you aware that in the post-war analyses were you aware of any information that there were, in fact, units of volunteers within the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. I did not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the sake of speed can I show you a document and ask if you are aware of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is: Were you aware of this, that there were units composed of volunteers or volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a page for this, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Page 56. Page 56 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This -- I'm afraid I don't have the page in your language, so I'll read it to you because time is going. This is an order of the commander of the 2nd Motorised Brigade to the -- it seems here to the command of the 2nd motorised -- of the 2nd Company command in which he says: "Immediately return the platoon of volunteers - Phantoms to put to the position because you have endangered the right flank of the adjacent unit." Just quickly. Did you ever hear of a platoon of volunteers referred to as the Phantoms?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not hear of such a platoon of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Paragraph 30 of your report says that Colonel Petkovic familiarised the volunteers with international humanitarian law because as a member of UN forces in Sinai he had knowledge in that area. Perhaps it might be a bit difficult with the translation. Could you slowly read what you have in paragraph 30 just to confirm the translation, please.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: "My deputy, Colonel Petkovic, familiarised them with provisions of international humanitarian law because as a member of the UN international forces in Sinai he was very well-versed in that area."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When -- what year did he go to the Sinai, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO KOSTIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, could you look, please, at paragraphs 14 and 15 of your report -- your statement. Could you read paragraph 14, please, read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President: "Training for anti-sabotage terrorist actions was the main focus of training in every unit, especially for specialised and strike military units in the zone of the Pristina Corps. This theme was one of the frequent contents that methodical-demonstrative exercises organized for officers and commands dealt with."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look now, please, at paragraph 26. Have you any recollection of who the personnel from OSCE were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the operations centre you mean, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you who the -- if you know who the personnel in the OSCE team were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps the witness should hear the OSCE interpreted as OEBS because he is listening to the interpretation here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know who was on the OSCE team. We were doing our best for them not to find out that the forward command post of the 3rd Army was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you allow them to enter the command post and carry out an inspection inside the premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, they did not go inside the command post of the 3rd Army. They just parked their car outside the command post. It was a concrete surface on which they parked their car, and below the concrete surface was the command post of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you know that they came to inspect the arms in the barracks in Kursumlija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found out from the barracks commander, that is, the brigade commander. It was a planned activity that was announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were they aware that they were parked on top of the command post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose so. How else could we explain that that precise location was struck by three air bombs and destroyed, the command post?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you were not aware of them asking for entry to the premises at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which premises do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The command post to count the arms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
